recipes.title: Chicken Tortilla Soup
recipes.blurb: The real Mexican version, where you char the tomatoes and toast the chiles, blend them, and fry the puree before adding broth. It takes about an hour and a half and tastes like nothing that comes from a jar of salsa.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) ripe roma tomatoes, about 6
1/2 large white onion (about 5 oz / 140 g), peeled and left in one piece
3 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed and seeded
1 dried chipotle or 1 canned chipotle in adobo
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 1/4 lb (570 g) boneless skinless chicken thighs
1 sprig fresh epazote, or 4 sprigs cilantro with stems
6 corn tortillas (6 in / 15 cm), cut into 1/4 in (6 mm) strips
1/2 cup (120 ml) neutral oil, for frying
3 oz (85 g) queso fresco or cotija, crumbled
1/2 cup (120 ml) Mexican crema or sour cream

instructions.title: Char the vegetables
instructions.text: Set a dry cast iron skillet or comal over medium-high heat and lay in the whole tomatoes, the onion half, and the unpeeled garlic cloves. Turn them every few minutes for 10 to 12 minutes, until the tomatoes are blistered and blackened in patches and slumping, the onion is charred on both cut faces, and the garlic skins are browned. Those black spots are flavor, not mistakes — this dry charring is what gives the soup its smoky depth. Pull the garlic early at about 6 minutes so it does not turn bitter.

instructions.title: Toast the chiles
instructions.text: In the same dry skillet over medium heat, press the guajillos flat for 20 to 30 seconds per side until they puff and smell like dried fruit. Move them straight into a bowl of hot water to soak for 15 minutes. Watch them closely; scorched chile turns the whole pot acrid and there is no rescuing it.

instructions.title: Blend the base
instructions.text: Peel the garlic and put it in a blender with the charred tomatoes and onion, the drained soaked guajillos, the chipotle, the 1 tsp oregano, and 1 tsp of the salt. Blend on high for 90 seconds until completely smooth. Add 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the broth if the blender struggles to catch. The puree should be brick red and thick like a loose sauce.

instructions.title: Fry the puree
instructions.text: Heat the 3 tbsp oil in a 5 qt (4.7 L) pot over medium-high until it shimmers, then pour in the blended puree — it will spit, so stand back and use a splatter screen. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens several shades, thickens to the consistency of tomato paste, and a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail. This frying step is the heart of the recipe: it cooks off raw blender flavor and concentrates everything into a real sauce base.

instructions.title: Add the broth
instructions.text: Pour in the 6 cups (1.4 L) chicken broth, stirring to dissolve the fried base completely, and add the epazote or cilantro sprigs. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 10 minutes so the flavors join up. The broth should be a rich rusty red with a slick of chile oil on the surface.

instructions.title: Poach the chicken
instructions.text: Slide in the chicken thighs, lower the heat so the surface barely trembles, and poach for 15 to 18 minutes. Check the thickest piece with an instant-read thermometer — it must reach 165°F (74°C), and thighs stay tender even a bit beyond that. A hard boil would seize the meat and cloud your broth, so keep it gentle.

instructions.title: Shred and return
instructions.text: Lift the chicken thighs onto a board with tongs, let them rest 5 minutes, then pull them apart into bite-sized shreds with two forks. Resting first lets the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb their juices, so they end up in the soup instead of running out onto the cutting board. Return the meat and every drop of collected juice to the pot. Shredding rather than chopping also gives the broth more surface to cling to, so each spoonful tastes seasoned.

instructions.title: Fry the tortilla strips
instructions.text: Heat the 1/2 cup (120 ml) oil in a small skillet to 350°F (175°C) — a strip dropped in should bubble immediately and vigorously. Fry the tortilla strips in three batches for 60 to 90 seconds each, until stiff and just barely golden, then drain on paper towels and salt them right away while the oil is still wet. Crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and gives you greasy limp strips instead of crisp ones.

instructions.title: Season the soup
instructions.text: Remove the epazote sprig, stir in the 2 tbsp lime juice and the remaining 1/2 tsp of the salt, and taste. Add more salt 1/4 tsp at a time until the chile flavor comes forward — this soup takes more salt than people expect because the chiles and tomatoes are both mild. It should taste smoky, tangy, and just a little spicy.

instructions.title: Build the bowls
instructions.text: Put a generous handful of tortilla strips in the bottom of each warm bowl, then ladle the hot soup over them so they soften slightly but keep some crunch. Top with diced avocado, crumbled queso fresco, a drizzle of crema, and more strips. Serve with lime wedges and eat it right away, before the strips give up entirely.

tips: Do not skip frying the blended puree. Pouring raw blended tomato straight into broth gives you thin, sour soup — the 8 minute fry is what makes it taste restaurant-made.
Short on time, bake the tortilla strips instead: toss with 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and bake at 400°F (205°C) for 10 to 12 minutes, tossing once.
Make the fried base up to 5 days ahead and refrigerate it, or freeze it for 3 months. Then dinner is just broth, chicken, and toppings.
Guajillos are mild and fruity, chipotle brings the smoke and heat. Add a second chipotle if you like it hot, or leave it out entirely and the soup still works.
Leftovers keep 4 days, but store the tortilla strips and toppings separately at room temperature or they turn to mush.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken thighs must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, poached at a bare simmer around 190°F (88°C). Fry the tortilla strips in oil held at 350°F (175°C) so they crisp rather than absorb grease.
recipes.pairing: A cold Mexican lager with lime, or a tamarind agua fresca, and warm corn tortillas on the side.

recipes.title: Split Pea Soup with Ham Hock
recipes.blurb: Cheap, humble, and quietly one of the best things you can make from a bag of dried peas and a smoked ham hock. It thickens itself, needs almost no attention, and feeds you for days.

items: 1 lb (450 g) dried green split peas
3 tbsp (42 g) unsalted butter, divided (2 tbsp for the pot, 1 tbsp for the croutons)
1 large yellow onion (about 10 oz / 280 g), diced
1 1/2 lb (680 g) smoked ham hock, or 1 leftover ham bone
8 cups (1.9 L) water or low-sodium chicken broth
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 cups (60 g) crusty bread cubes, for croutons

instructions.title: Sort and rinse the peas
instructions.text: Spread the split peas on a sheet pan and pick out any small stones, shriveled peas, or bits of debris — bagged legumes genuinely do contain the occasional pebble and it will crack a tooth. Rinse them in a colander under cold water until the water runs clear. Unlike beans, split peas do not need soaking; they break down on their own in about 90 minutes.

instructions.title: Build the aromatic base
instructions.text: Melt the 2 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a 6 qt (5.7 L) pot over medium heat, then add the onion, carrots, celery, and 1 tsp salt. Cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the onion is translucent and the vegetables are soft with a little gold at the edges. This is the flavor floor of the soup, and 5 minutes is not enough. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more.

instructions.title: Add the peas and hock
instructions.text: Stir in the rinsed split peas and coat them in the fat for a minute, then add the ham hock, the 8 cups (1.9 L) water or broth, the bay leaves, and the thyme sprigs. Use water rather than broth if your hock is a good smoky one; it gives you plenty of flavor and lets the peas taste like themselves. Bring it up to a boil.

instructions.title: Skim and settle into a simmer
instructions.text: Once it boils, skim off the gray foam that rises with a shallow spoon and discard it. Lower the heat until the surface bubbles lazily, around 200°F (93°C), and set the lid slightly ajar. A hard boil scorches the peas on the bottom and makes the whole pot taste burnt, which is the classic split pea failure.

instructions.title: Simmer and stir the bottom
instructions.text: Cook for 75 to 90 minutes, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes and dragging your spoon flat across the bottom of the pot. Split peas sink and stick as they break down, so that scrape is not optional. Add hot water 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time if the soup gets thicker than you want before the peas are done.

instructions.title: Check the peas
instructions.text: The soup is ready when the peas have completely lost their shape and dissolved into a thick, pale green puree with no gritty texture on your tongue. If they still feel firm at 90 minutes, your peas were old — keep simmering and check every 15 minutes, since stale legumes can take twice as long. Old peas are the only real risk in this recipe.

instructions.title: Pull and shred the hock
instructions.text: Lift the ham hock out with tongs onto a board and let it cool 10 minutes. Pull the meat off the bone, discard the skin, fat, and gristle, and chop the meat into bite-sized pieces — expect about 1 1/2 cups (8 oz / 225 g). The meat is fully cooked and pulls away easily once the collagen has broken down, which happens well past 195°F (91°C).

instructions.title: Decide on the texture
instructions.text: Remove the bay leaves and thyme stems. For a rustic soup, leave it as is; for a smoother one, blend about half with an immersion blender or pulse it a few times. If you use a countertop blender, fill it no more than halfway and vent the lid with a towel, because hot puree will blow the lid off a sealed jar.

instructions.title: Return the meat and adjust
instructions.text: Stir the chopped ham back in and warm it through over low heat for 5 minutes so the meat picks up the soup and the soup picks up the smoke. Split pea soup thickens dramatically as it sits, so thin it with hot water or broth, 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time, until it flows off a spoon in a thick ribbon rather than plopping. Aim slightly looser than you actually want it in the bowl. Remember it will be noticeably thicker again by tomorrow, and thicker still the day after.

instructions.title: Season and serve
instructions.text: Add the 1 tsp black pepper and the 2 tsp cider vinegar, then taste before salting — smoked hocks vary wildly and some are salty enough that you need none at all. The vinegar cuts the starchy heaviness and makes the smoke taste sharper. Toss the 2 cups bread cubes in a skillet with the reserved 1 tbsp butter over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until golden, and scatter them over each bowl with a grind of extra pepper.

tips: The bone from a holiday ham is even better than a store-bought hock, and it is free. Freeze it after Easter or Christmas specifically for this pot.
For a vegetarian version, skip the hock, use vegetable broth, and add 1 1/2 tsp smoked paprika plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) soy sauce to replace the smoke and savoriness.
It thickens into something closer to spackle in the fridge. That is normal — reheat with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of water or broth per two servings, stirring over medium-low.
Freezes for 3 months. Freeze in flat zip bags and thaw in a bowl of cold water in about 30 minutes.
Never salt heavily at the start. The hock releases salt over 90 minutes, and a pot seasoned early can end up inedible by the time it is done.
recipes.keyTemp: There is no doneness temperature for the peas — they are ready when they have dissolved completely and feel smooth, not gritty, after 75-90 minutes at a bare simmer near 200°F (93°C). The smoked hock is already cooked and shreds easily once its collagen breaks down above 195°F (91°C).
recipes.pairing: Buttered rye toast or garlic croutons, with a cold pilsner or a cup of strong tea.

recipes.title: Chicken and Andouille Gumbo
recipes.blurb: It starts with forty-five minutes of stirring flour and oil until it turns the color of dark chocolate, and everything good about this dish comes from that. Serve it over rice and it will ruin every other gumbo for you.

items: 2 1/2 lb (1.1 kg) bone-in skin-on chicken thighs, about 6
2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 lb (450 g) andouille sausage, sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) thick
1 cup (240 ml) neutral oil such as canola or peanut
2 large onions (about 20 oz / 570 g), finely diced
2 green bell peppers (about 14 oz / 400 g), finely diced
1 tsp cayenne pepper, or to taste
1 tsp hot sauce such as Crystal or Tabasco, plus more for the table
1 tsp file powder, for the table (optional)
6 cups (1 kg) cooked long-grain white rice, for serving

instructions.title: Prep absolutely everything first
instructions.text: Dice all the vegetables, measure the flour and oil, warm the stock, and set every bowl within arm's reach of the stove before you turn on a burner. Once the roux starts you cannot leave it for even 60 seconds, and a roux that burns has to be thrown out and started over. This is the one recipe in the book where mise en place is genuinely non-negotiable.

instructions.title: Season and brown the chicken
instructions.text: Pat the thighs dry and season with the 2 tsp salt and 1 tsp pepper. Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a heavy 8 qt (7.6 L) Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the thighs skin-side down for 6 to 7 minutes without moving them, then 3 minutes on the second side. They will not be cooked through and that is fine. Move them to a plate.

instructions.title: Brown the andouille
instructions.text: Add the sliced andouille to the same pot and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the edges are browned and the pot has picked up more fond. Scoop the sausage out with a slotted spoon and set it with the chicken. Pour off all the accumulated fat and wipe the pot with a paper towel — the roux needs clean oil and an even, unmarked surface so you can read its color.

instructions.title: Start the roux
instructions.text: Add the 1 cup (240 ml) oil to the pot over medium heat until it shimmers, then whisk in the 1 cup (120 g) flour all at once until completely smooth with no dry pockets. Switch to a flat wooden spoon or heatproof spatula so you can scrape the corners. From this moment forward, stir constantly and never stop. Hot roux is called Cajun napalm for a reason; keep children and pets out of the kitchen and wear long sleeves.

instructions.title: Work through the color stages
instructions.text: Over 35 to 45 minutes at medium to medium-low heat, the roux moves through recognizable stages: blond and smelling like pancakes at 10 minutes, peanut butter at 20, copper penny at 30, and finally dark chocolate at 40. Keep the spoon moving across the entire bottom in a figure eight, never letting it rest. If you see black flecks or smell anything acrid and burnt, stop and start over — burnt roux poisons the entire pot and cannot be salvaged.

instructions.title: Judge the finish
instructions.text: You are aiming for the color of melted dark chocolate or an old copper penny, smelling deeply toasted and nutty. The darker it goes the more flavor it gives and the less it thickens, which is why classic gumbo is soupy rather than gravy-thick. If your kitchen is nerve-wracking, stop at copper — a slightly lighter roux still makes very good gumbo, and burnt is unfixable.

instructions.title: Stop the roux with the trinity
instructions.text: The instant the roux hits the color you want, dump in all the onion, bell pepper, and celery at once and stir hard. The cold vegetables drop the temperature immediately and halt the browning, which is the only reliable way to stop a roux from carrying past done. It will hiss and steam dramatically. Cook 8 to 10 minutes until the vegetables are soft and the mixture looks like dark, glossy paste.

instructions.title: Add garlic and seasonings
instructions.text: Stir in the minced garlic, 2 tsp thyme, 1 1/2 tsp smoked paprika, and 1 tsp cayenne and cook for 60 to 90 seconds until fragrant. Ground spices need this brief hot fat contact to open up. Cayenne is where the heat lives, so start with a teaspoon and add more at the end if you want it hotter.

instructions.title: Whisk in the stock gradually
instructions.text: Add the warm stock 1 cup (240 ml) at a time, whisking each addition fully smooth before the next goes in. Adding cold stock all at once seizes the roux into stubborn lumps that never dissolve. Once all 10 cups (2.4 L) are in, the pot should look like thin dark gravy. Add the bay leaves, Worcestershire, and hot sauce.

instructions.title: Simmer and skim
instructions.text: Return the browned sausage to the pot, bring to a simmer, then lower the heat so it barely bubbles and cook uncovered for 1 hour. Orange oil will rise to the surface — skim most of it off with a wide shallow spoon every 20 minutes. Some old-school cooks leave it, but skimming gives a cleaner, more balanced gumbo. Stir the bottom occasionally.

instructions.title: Cook the chicken through
instructions.text: Nestle the chicken thighs back in with their juices and simmer 30 minutes more, until an instant-read thermometer in the thickest thigh reads at least 165°F (74°C); dark meat is even better around 175°F (79°C). Lift them out, discard the skin and bones, shred the meat, and return it to the pot. The gumbo should now be the color of strong coffee with cream.

instructions.title: Finish and serve over rice
instructions.text: Taste and adjust with salt, more cayenne, or another dash of hot sauce — gumbo needs assertive seasoning to stand up to plain rice. Stir in most of the scallions and parsley and let it sit off the heat for 15 minutes. Serve by mounding a scoop of hot rice in the center of each bowl and ladling the gumbo around it, topped with the remaining scallions. Pass file powder and hot sauce at the table, but never boil the gumbo after file goes in or it turns stringy.

tips: Use a flat-edged wooden spoon or spatula, not a whisk, once the roux gets dark. A flat edge scrapes the pot bottom where scorching starts, and that is exactly where a whisk cannot reach.

If you are nervous about stirring for 45 minutes, make an oven roux: whisk the oil and flour in a cast iron pot and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, stirring every 25 minutes. It is nearly foolproof and frees your hands.
Gumbo is definitively better on day two. Cool it, refrigerate overnight, lift off the fat cap, and reheat gently — the roux flavor rounds out and stops tasting sharp.
Never add file powder to the pot while it is on the heat. Sprinkle it over individual bowls at the table, where it thickens and adds an earthy root beer note without going ropey.
No andouille? Use kielbasa plus an extra 1/2 tsp smoked paprika and 1/4 tsp cayenne. It is not the same, but it is good.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of the thigh, with 175°F (79°C) giving more tender dark meat. The roux itself runs above 350°F (175°C) and will cause severe burns — treat it with real caution and never leave it unattended.
recipes.pairing: Cold Abita Amber or any crisp lager, with potato salad on the side the way they do it in south Louisiana.

recipes.title: Shoyu Ramen with Chicken Broth
recipes.blurb: A clear, golden chicken and pork broth built over four hours, seasoned bowl by bowl with a soy tare you make yourself. It is a real project, and the first sip explains exactly why people bother.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) chicken backs, wings, and feet if you can get them
1 lb (450 g) pork neck bones or trotter, split
16 cups (3.8 L) cold water for the broth, plus 3 cups (720 ml) for the kombu dashi, 1/2 cup (120 ml) for the egg marinade, and more for parboiling
1 piece fresh ginger (2 in / 5 cm), sliced
1/3 cup (80 ml) chicken fat or neutral oil
4 portions fresh ramen noodles (about 4 oz / 115 g each)
8 oz (225 g) sliced chashu pork or roast pork belly (optional)
1/2 cup (25 g) thinly sliced scallion greens, for topping
2 tbsp (30 ml) chili oil, for the table

instructions.title: Cold-soak the kombu and shiitake
instructions.text: Put the 10 g kombu and the dried shiitake in a bowl with 3 cups (720 ml) of cold water and leave them in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or overnight if you plan ahead. Cold extraction pulls glutamates out of kombu without the slimy, faintly fishy edge that boiling it produces. This dashi becomes part of your broth later, so save every drop.

instructions.title: Parboil the bones
instructions.text: Put all the chicken and pork bones in your largest stockpot, cover with cold water, and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Boil hard for 10 minutes — a thick gray scum will foam up and look genuinely alarming. Drain everything into the sink and rinse each bone under cold running water, scrubbing off any clinging coagulated blood. Skipping this step is why homemade ramen broth often looks muddy and tastes like a barnyard.

instructions.title: Scrub the pot too
instructions.text: Wash the pot itself before the bones go back in, since scum sticks to the sides in a gray ring and will redissolve into your clean broth if you leave it there. Return the scrubbed bones and add the 16 cups (3.8 L) fresh cold water. Everything should be covered by about 2 in (5 cm); add water if it is not, because bones that poke above the surface dry out and contribute nothing. Starting over with cold water rather than hot also lets you catch any last foam as it rises.

instructions.title: Bring it up slowly
instructions.text: Set the pot over medium heat and let it come to a bare simmer over 30 minutes rather than blasting it. As it heats, skim any remaining foam from the surface with a fine mesh skimmer. For this clear chintan style broth you want a lazy bubble breaking every second or two, around 190°F (88°C) — a hard boil emulsifies the fat and turns the broth cloudy and greasy.

instructions.title: Simmer for three hours
instructions.text: Hold that bare simmer, uncovered or with the lid cracked, for 3 hours. Check every 30 minutes and top up with hot water if the bones become exposed. The broth will slowly turn pale gold and start to smell rich and clean, and it should feel slightly sticky between your fingertips from the gelatin.

instructions.title: Add the aromatics late
instructions.text: In the final 45 minutes, add the halved onion, sliced ginger, smashed garlic, and scallion whites, plus the soaked shiitake and their soaking liquid. Add the kombu only for the last 20 minutes and pull it before it goes slippery. Aromatics added at the start would simmer into bitterness over three hours, so they always go in late.

instructions.title: Make the shoyu tare
instructions.text: While the broth finishes, combine the 1 cup (240 ml) soy sauce, 1/3 cup (80 ml) mirin, 2 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp sugar, and the 5 g kombu in a small saucepan and warm it to just below a simmer, about 180°F (82°C), for 10 minutes. Turn off the heat, add the katsuobushi, and let it steep 15 minutes before straining. You should end up with about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), which is exactly what you need: 1/2 cup (120 ml) for the eggs and roughly 3 tbsp (45 ml) per bowl. The tare is the seasoning of the entire bowl — the broth itself stays unsalted so you can dial each bowl exactly.

instructions.title: Make the aroma oil
instructions.text: Warm the 1/3 cup (80 ml) chicken fat or oil in a small pan over medium-low with the sliced scallion greens for 6 to 8 minutes, until the scallions are frizzled and the oil smells sweet and oniony. Strain out the solids. That layer of flavored fat floating on the finished bowl is what traps the aroma and keeps the soup blazing hot to the last spoonful.

instructions.title: Cook the marinated eggs
instructions.text: Lower room-temperature eggs into boiling water with a spoon and boil for exactly 6 minutes and 30 seconds for a jammy, barely-set yolk. Move them straight into ice water for 5 minutes, peel carefully, then submerge them in 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the tare thinned with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water for at least 2 hours or overnight. The ice bath stops the cooking cold; even 30 extra seconds gives you a chalky yolk.

instructions.title: Strain and finish the broth
instructions.text: Strain the broth through a fine mesh sieve into a clean pot, pressing gently on the solids, then strain again through a sieve lined with a paper towel if you want it crystal clear. You should have 8 to 10 cups (1.9 to 2.4 L). Skim the fat from the top and save it for aroma oil. Keep the broth hot, right around 195°F (91°C) — ramen must be served scaldingly hot or it dies in the bowl.

instructions.title: Taste and set the salinity
instructions.text: Test one bowl before committing: start with 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) of tare and 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of hot broth, then taste. It should be assertively savory, just this side of too salty, because the noodles are unsalted and will dilute it. Adjust up or down by the tablespoon and use that ratio for every bowl.

instructions.title: Set up before the noodles
instructions.text: Heat your serving bowls with hot tap water and dry them, then line up all the toppings — halved eggs, chashu, nori, sliced scallions. Ramen assembly takes 90 seconds and there is no time to hunt for anything. Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a rolling boil for the noodles.

instructions.title: Boil the noodles and build
instructions.text: Cook the fresh ramen noodles for 60 to 90 seconds, or exactly as the package says, then lift them out and shake them completely dry in the strainer. Put the tare and 1 tbsp (15 ml) aroma oil in the bottom of each hot bowl, pour in the hot broth, then lower in the drained noodles and lift them with chopsticks into a neat fold. Any water clinging to the noodles waters down the broth you spent four hours on. Top with the egg, chashu, nori tucked against the rim, and scallions, and eat immediately.

tips: Make the broth, tare, and aroma oil up to 4 days ahead, or freeze the broth for 3 months. Then a bowl of ramen is a 10 minute weeknight dinner.
Chicken feet look strange but they are the single best source of gelatin, and they are what gives ramen broth its body. Ask the butcher counter — they are usually cheap.
Never salt the broth itself. Every element of a ramen bowl is seasoned by the tare, which is how shops adjust each bowl and how you avoid an oversalted pot you cannot undo.
Fresh ramen noodles from an Asian market are worth the trip. If you can only find dried, cook them a minute shy of the package time so they finish in the hot broth.
If your broth comes out cloudy, the heat was too high. It will still taste good, but next time watch for the bubble that breaks only every second or two.
recipes.keyTemp: Hold the broth at a bare simmer of 185-195°F (85-91°C) for the full 3 hours — boiling makes it cloudy. Marinated eggs need exactly 6 1/2 minutes in boiling water then an ice bath, and any chicken meat used as topping must reach 165°F (74°C).
recipes.pairing: Cold Japanese lager or barley tea, with gyoza on the side and chili oil at the table.
